questions.q: What does it mean that TypeScript is a "superset" of JavaScript?
questions.explain: "Superset" is about syntax. let balance = 5000; balance = "empty"; is valid JavaScript and valid TypeScript syntax, but it fails the type check. Programs still run as JavaScript; TypeScript never has its own engine.
options: Every JavaScript program passes the TypeScript type check
Every piece of JavaScript syntax is also TypeScript syntax, and TypeScript adds more syntax on top
TypeScript runs faster than JavaScript because it is compiled
TypeScript replaces JavaScript at runtime with a typed engine

questions.q: Why is TypeScript's checking called static?
questions.explain: Static analysis reads the source text and works out types for every expression. Dynamic checks, like JavaScript's TypeError, only happen on lines that actually run.
options: Because types never change once written
Because it only checks static class members
Because the code is analysed without running it
Because it happens while the server is idle

questions.q: A project runs its server with node src/server.ts in production and tsx src/server.ts in development. Which step in this setup finds type errors?
questions.explain: Node's type stripping and tsx both remove types and run the rest. Neither asks whether the types are right. Without a tsc --noEmit step, a type error can reach production.
options: Both, but only for files that are imported
None of them. Only tsc (or the editor running the same checker) checks types.

questions.q: You run npx tsc --noEmit false --outDir dist on a project with one type error, and no other settings. What happens?
questions.explain: Checking and emitting are independent. By default tsc writes the JavaScript anyway and signals it with exit code 2. Turn on noEmitOnError to stop it writing anything while there are errors.
options: Nothing is written, and tsc exits with 1
The error is printed, the .js files are still written, and tsc exits with 2
The error is printed and only the files without errors are written
The line with the error is left out of the output

questions.q: Your CI runs npm run check && npm test, where check is tsc --noEmit. There is a type error. What happens to the tests?
questions.explain: tsc --noEmit exits with 1 when it finds errors. a && b runs b only when a exited with 0, so a type error stops the chain. That is what makes the check a gate.
options: They run, because --noEmit writes nothing and so cannot fail
They do not run: tsc exits with a non-zero code, and && only runs the next command after a zero exit code
They run, but only the tests for the files without errors
They run first, because && runs both commands at the same time

questions.q: When does "noEmitOnError": true make a difference?
questions.explain: It does not change what is checked. It only decides whether files are written when the check fails. In a check-only project (noEmit) nothing is written anyway.
options: Always; it makes the checker stricter
Only when "noEmit": true is also set
Only when tsc is writing files: it then writes nothing while there are errors

questions.q: Which of these survives in the JavaScript that tsc emits?
questions.explain: A default parameter value is JavaScript, so it stays: currency = "NGN". as, satisfies, ! and the annotation : Currency are type syntax and are erased without a trace.

questions.q: What does import { transferFee, type Transfer } from "./transfer.js"; become in the emitted JavaScript?
questions.explain: Only the part marked type is removed. transferFee is a real function, so its import stays. If the whole import were import type { … }, the whole line would go.
options: Nothing: the whole line is removed

questions.q: Which of these makes tsc generate new JavaScript code that was not in your file?
questions.explain: A parameter property (private, public, protected or readonly on a constructor parameter) makes tsc write a class field and this.balance = balance;. The others are erased completely.

questions.q: What does the erasableSyntaxOnly setting do?
questions.explain: With it on, the checker refuses the syntax that type-stripping tools such as Node.js cannot handle. You find out at check time instead of when the server fails to start.
options: It makes tsc remove all types, even from .d.ts files
It reports an error (TS1294) for syntax that needs generated code, such as enum, namespace and parameter properties
It makes Node.js check types while stripping them
It turns every enum into a union type automatically

questions.q: With "target": "ES2019", tsc rewrites order.discount?.percent ?? 0 into a long expression with === null and void 0. Why?
questions.explain: That translation between versions of the same language is transpiling. ?. and ?? are JavaScript (ES2020), not TypeScript; with a modern target they are left as they are.
options: Because optional chaining is a TypeScript feature that must be erased
Because ?. and ?? were added in ES2020, so they must be translated into syntax an ES2019 engine understands
Because the checker found a possible undefined
Because ES2019 has no template literals

questions.q: Your target is ES2019 and you call amounts.findLast(…), an ES2023 array method. What happens?
questions.explain: target rewrites syntax but never adds functions (polyfills). Its default lib matches the target, so the checker reports TS2550 and suggests a newer lib.
options: tsc adds a copy of findLast to the output
tsc rewrites the call into a loop
tsc reports that findLast does not exist on the array type, because the target also decides which built-in functions it assumes
Nothing, until the code runs on an old engine

questions.q: What is in a .d.ts file that tsc --declaration writes for a module with one exported function?
questions.explain: A declaration file holds only types. Packages ship .js for running and .d.ts so that editors and tsc know every exported function's parameters and return type.
options: The compiled JavaScript of the function
The function's signature (export declare function …) with no body
A source map from JavaScript back to TypeScript
A copy of the .ts file with comments removed

questions.q: A production server runs node dist/main.js. Error stack traces in the logs point at dist/main.js:3:15, which is hard to relate to the source. What fixes that?
questions.explain: A source map maps positions in the emitted JavaScript back to the .ts file. With --enable-source-maps, Node uses it, and stack traces name main.ts and the line you wrote.
options: Emitting source maps (sourceMap) and starting Node with --enable-source-maps

questions.q: What does npx tsc --noEmit --watch do?
questions.explain: Watch mode is a long-running checker. With --noEmit it writes nothing. It does not run your program; you pair it with something like node --watch or tsx watch in a second terminal.
options: Runs your program and restarts it on every change
Checks the project once, then keeps running and re-checks whenever a file is saved
Checks only the files that are open in your editor
Writes .js files every time you save

questions.q: With Node.js type stripping, import { Transfer } from "./types.ts" fails at startup with "does not provide an export named 'Transfer'", where Transfer is an interface. Why?
questions.explain: Writing import type { Transfer } tells every tool the import can be deleted. verbatimModuleSyntax makes tsc require it (TS1484), so the checker catches this before Node does.
options: Node.js does not support imports in .ts files
Node strips each file on its own, cannot know Transfer is only a type, keeps the import, and the other file has no such runtime export
The file extension must be .js, not .ts
Interfaces must be exported with export default

questions.q: A project runs with plain node src/main.ts and also compiles with tsc for production. Which pair of settings lets you write import { transferFee } from "./fees.ts" in the source and still get ./fees.js in the emitted JavaScript?
questions.explain: Node needs the real file name, ./fees.ts. allowImportingTsExtensions lets the checker accept that path, and rewriteRelativeImportExtensions makes tsc change it to ./fees.js when it emits.

questions.q: Which statement about node file.ts in Node.js 24 is true?
questions.explain: Node's type stripping has no configuration from tsconfig.json, never checks types, and refuses to strip files inside node_modules. That is why packages are published as compiled JavaScript.
options: It refuses to run a file that has a type error

questions.q: What does the <Transfer> in parseJson<Transfer>(text) do at runtime?
questions.explain: Type arguments only shape what the compiler believes about the result. After erasure, parseJson is just JSON.parse, whatever T you wrote.
options: It checks that the parsed object has the properties of Transfer
It converts string numbers into numbers
Nothing: it is erased, so every call runs the same plain function
It throws if the JSON does not match

questions.q: Why does type Currency = "NGN" | "USD"; Currency.includes(code) fail with TS2693?
questions.explain: Types are erased, so there is nothing to call includes on. Start from a value instead, const currencies = ["NGN", "USD"] as const, and derive the type with (typeof currencies)[number].
options: Because Currency is only a type and does not exist at runtime, so it cannot be used as a value
Because includes is not available on the target

questions.q: A type test contains // @ts-expect-error above transferFee("2500");. One day someone changes transferFee(amount: number) to transferFee(amount: any). What does tsc --noEmit do?
questions.explain: @ts-expect-error demands an error on the next line. When the type was loosened to any, the error disappeared, and the unused directive became the error. That is how a type test catches a weakened type.
options: Nothing, because the directive silences the line
Reports TS2578 "Unused '@ts-expect-error' directive", because the line no longer has an error

questions.q: const limit: number = Number(env.TRANSFER_LIMIT) compiles. The variable is set to "5O000" (letter O). Why can the compiler not warn you?
questions.explain: The compiler knows the variable's type (string | undefined), never its content. Number("5O000") is NaN, whose type is number. Only a runtime check can refuse it.
options: Because the text is only known at runtime, and NaN is a perfectly valid value of type number
Because strict is off for environment variables
Because Number("5O000") throws before the compiler can see it

questions.q: With limit = NaN, which check refuses every transfer (fails closed) instead of allowing every transfer (fails open)?
questions.explain: Every comparison with NaN is false. amount <= NaN is false, so the code refuses. amount > NaN is also false, so "refuse when above" never refuses, and !(amount > NaN) always allows. Even better: validate the limit when you read it, so it can never be NaN.

questions.q: Which package.json script is the one that must run in CI for type errors to block a release?
questions.explain: Only tsc checks types. Vitest, like tsx, strips types and runs the tests without checking them.

questions.q: This is the refund code after the types have been stripped. What does it print?
questions.explain: With a string on one side, + joins text: 1000 + "25" is "100025". TypeScript would have refused the call, but stripping types does not check them.

questions.q: The annotation says amount is a number. What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON.parse returns any, so the annotation is trusted, not checked. At runtime amount is the string "5". * converts it to a number (10), while + joins text ("52"). console.log prints both without quotes.
questions.code:
const transfer: { amount: number } = JSON.parse('{"amount": "5"}');

console.log(transfer.amount * 2, transfer.amount + 2);

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: as number is erased. It tells the compiler to treat the value as a number; it does not convert it. At runtime amount is still the string "2500".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The type argument <Transfer> is erased; nothing compares the JSON with the interface. amount is the string "700", and + 50 joins text.
options: It throws: the JSON does not match Transfer

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: "5O000" contains a letter, so Number gives NaN. Every comparison with NaN is false, in both directions. Number.isNaN is the reliable test.
questions.code:
const limit = Number("5O000");

console.log(20000 > limit, 20000 <= limit, Number.isNaN(limit));

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The ! tells the compiler "this is not undefined" and is then erased. No check runs, so first is undefined, exactly what find returned.

questions.q: An enum generates a real object. What does this print?
questions.explain: A numeric enum becomes an object with both directions: Status.Pending is 0, and Status[1] is the name "Settled". Because it is a real object, typeof gives "object". That generated code is why Node's type stripping refuses enums.
options: It throws: Status is only a type

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Parameter properties generate real fields and assignments. private is only a compile-time rule, so balance is an ordinary property at runtime and Object.keys lists it.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Only the annotations are erased. The default value = 0.01 is JavaScript and stays in the emitted code, so fee(5000) uses it.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A class is also a runtime value (a function), so typeof and instanceof work with it. An interface leaves nothing behind: r is just an object.

questions.q: This is the erasable replacement for an enum. What does it print?
questions.explain: The const object is plain JavaScript and survives; the type with the same name is erased. Object.values gives only the two strings, with no reverse mapping.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Number("") is 0, which the value <= 0 rule refuses. Number("1e3") is 1000 (scientific notation), which passes. Runtime checks must think about what Number really accepts.

questions.q: Write readLimit(raw: string | undefined): number. It returns the number when raw is a positive whole number, and throws Error("invalid limit: " + raw) otherwise. The loop should then print the results shown.
questions.explain: Number.isInteger rejects NaN and decimals in one go. The compiler cannot do this check for you: it only knows the value is a string | undefined.
questions.expected:
50000
invalid limit: 5O000
invalid limit: undefined
invalid limit: -1

questions.q: Replace the enum with an erasable const object plus a type of the same name, so the file would run under node file.ts. Keep the label function working. It should print pending -> settled.
questions.explain: as const keeps the exact strings, and (typeof Status)[keyof typeof Status] is the union "pending" | "settled". Callers still write Status.Pending, and deleting the types leaves valid JavaScript.

questions.q: Rewrite the class without parameter properties: declare the fields and assign them in the constructor. It should print Ada: ₦5000.
questions.explain: This is exactly the JavaScript tsc would have generated for the parameter properties, written by you. With erasableSyntaxOnly, it is the only form allowed.

questions.q: Start from a runtime array of supported currencies and derive the Currency type from it. Write isSupported(code: string): boolean using the array. Print true false for "GBP" and "EUR".
questions.explain: The type cannot be checked at runtime because it is erased. The array can. Deriving the type from the array keeps one list for both worlds.

questions.q: Settings arrive as text. Write parseAmount(text: string): number that returns a whole number of naira and throws Error("not an amount: " + text) for anything else (including empty text). Use it so the refund prints the numbers shown.
questions.explain: Converting at the edge, with a check, turns outside text into a trustworthy number before any arithmetic happens. The empty-text test matters because Number("") is 0.

questions.q: Write decide(amount: number, limit: number): string that returns "allowed", "refused", or "limit invalid" when limit is not a positive finite number. It must never allow a transfer when the limit is broken.
questions.explain: The starter fails open: 9000 > NaN is false, so it allows. Checking the limit first, and allowing only when amount <= limit is true, makes the code fail closed.

questions.q: Write parseTransfer(json: string): Transfer that checks at runtime that from and to are strings and amount is a positive number, and throws Error("invalid transfer") otherwise.
questions.explain: Storing the parse result as unknown forces checks before use. After the typeof checks, TypeScript knows each field's real type, and the returned object is built from checked values only.

questions.q: Write readPort(env: Record<string, string | undefined>): number. PORT is optional (default 3000); when given it must be a whole number from 1 to 65535, otherwise throw Error("PORT must be 1-65535").
questions.explain: Environment variables are text that arrives at runtime. The type string | undefined makes you handle the missing case; the range check handles the nonsense case, which no type can express.

questions.q: A partner sends a JSON array of transfer amounts. Some entries are broken. Write totalFees(json: string): number that adds up transferFee(amount) for every entry that is a positive number and skips everything else. It should print 35.
questions.explain: The starter's number[] annotation is a promise about data it never checked, so "700", null and -5 are all charged a fee (the starter prints 65). Treating the parsed value as unknown and checking each item keeps only the 2500 (₦10) and the 20000 (₦25).
